intro: Where the two differ, every phrase is given twice: first in standard written Persian – correct, polite and understood everywhere – and then, marked 🗣, in the everyday spoken Persian of Tehran, which is what you will actually hear in shops, taxis and homes. Learn to say the spoken form and to recognise both. Persian has two words for 'you': shomā, for anyone you don't know well, anyone older than you and any official (it is also the plural), and to, for friends, family and children. Phrases marked formal use shomā – verbs end in -id, spoken -in – or the polite register; the others use to – verbs end in -i – and are for people you are close to. When in doubt, use shomā: nobody minds too much respect, and when an Iranian friend starts calling you to, you can answer in kind. Tap a phrase to hear it.

sections.title: Greetings and goodbyes
sections.intro: Salām works at any hour and with anyone, and the person who arrives says it first – a younger person greets an older one. Questions about your health and family follow straight away; they are part of the greeting, so answer briefly and ask back. Goodbyes take time: expect several rounds of good wishes at the door.

items.note: Works at any time of day and with anyone – shopkeepers, drivers, neighbours, officials.

items.en: Peace be upon you (a respectful hello).
items.note: More traditional, especially with older people. The reply is aleykom assalām.
From late afternoon until dark.
Said when you leave in the evening or go to bed – not as a greeting.
Iranians of every background say khodā ro shokr – it is as much habit as faith.
A casual follow-up to hello.
salāmati, 'health', is the standard answer to che khabar?

items.fa: خیلی وقت است شما را ندیده‌ام!
items.r: kheyli vaght ast shomā rā na-dide-am!

items.note: Literally 'you are rarely seen' – a friendly tease.
Literally 'God (be your) protector'.
A warm alternative to khodā hāfez, often said in reply to it.
Very casual, among friends.

sections.title: Introductions
sections.intro: Iranians ask personal questions early – your job, your age, whether you are married, what you think of Iran. It is friendliness, not nosiness; answer as much as you like. Use shomā with everyone you meet for the first time.

items.en: What's your name? (to a child or a friend)

items.note: Younger people often say khoshbakht-am.

items.en: Let me introduce my friend Ali.

items.note: In speech Engelis means England – and often the whole of Britain.

items.en: What do you do for a living?
items.note: You will also hear chi-kāre-in? – 'what do you do?'
A normal question in Iran, though asked less often to women.
Questions about marriage and children are ordinary small talk.

sections.title: Courtesy and ta'ārof
sections.intro: Ta'ārof is the ritual politeness that runs through Iranian life: offering what you don't expect to be accepted, refusing what you would like, insisting that the other person go first. The rule of thumb is to refuse an offer once or twice and accept the third time – and when a shopkeeper or driver says your money is 'not worthy', thank them and pay anyway.

items.note: The everyday thank-you, fine with anyone.
Borrowed from French; heard everywhere in the cities, a touch casual.
Thanks for something someone has made or done for you – a meal, a favour, a gift.
Also 'please' when you ask a favour.

items.lit: it is not worthy of you
items.note: Said when giving a present – and by shopkeepers and drivers when you ask the price. It is courtesy: insist, and pay.

items.en: That's kind of you. How much is it?
items.note: The right answer to ghābel na-dāre: thank them, then ask again.

items.en: Not at all! / Don't say that!
items.note: The polite protest when someone praises you or puts themselves down.
To get attention, to apologise, or to squeeze past.
Very common: for being late, for having no change, for a host's 'simple' dinner.

items.en: Please – go ahead / come in / sit down / help yourself.
items.note: The all-purpose polite invitation: when you hear it, step forward, sit, or take what is offered.
Iranians insist on going last through a door. After two rounds, go first and say be-bakhshid.
Said when you leave a room, take the last piece, or finally accept after ta'ārof.

items.en: Please don't be polite – really, take it.
items.note: A host's way of saying the offer is sincere.

items.en: You went to so much trouble. (Thank you.)
Please don't go to any trouble.
Thank you for your hard work!
items.note: Said to anyone working or just finished – a cashier, a driver at the end of the ride, a teacher after class.
The reply to khaste na-bāshid.
Also a warm way to end a phone call.
The polite yes to a request or an instruction.

sections.title: Understanding each other
sections.intro: Iranians are delighted when a foreigner tries Persian, and most will happily slow down, repeat and teach you a new word. Don't be shy about asking – and expect plenty of people to try out their English on you in return.

items.en: Do you understand? / Did you get that?

items.note: The warm, polite way to say 'pardon?' or to answer when someone calls you – much kinder than che? ('what?').

items.fa: این را به فارسی چه می‌گویند؟
items.r: in rā be fārsi che mi-guyand?

items.fa: این کلمه را چطور تلفظ می‌کنید؟
items.r: in kalame rā chetor talaffoz mi-konid?
items.en: How do you pronounce this word?
items.col: این کلمه رو چطوری تلفظ می‌کنین؟
items.colR: in kalame ro chetori talaffoz mi-konin?

items.en: Could you write it down for me?
Sorry, my Persian isn't very good.

sections.title: Numbers and money
sections.intro: Prices are written in rials but almost always spoken in tomans: one toman is ten rials, so a tag that says 500,000 rials means 50,000 tomans. In speech the 'thousand' is usually dropped as well, so if a price sounds impossibly low, ask 'tomans or rials?'. Foreign bank cards do not work in Iran: visitors bring cash to change, or buy a prepaid local card.

items.en: How much does it come to?
items.note: At the till, at the end of a taxi ride or a meal.
In speech the 'thousand' is usually dropped: panjāh tomen means 50,000 tomans.
In speech chahār is often chār.

items.en: twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred
a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand

items.note: Spoken, literally 'can I swipe a card?'. Card machines are everywhere, but they take only Iranian cards.

items.en: Do you have a card machine?
I'll send it by card-to-card transfer.
items.note: Iranians often pay each other by instant transfer to a card number.

items.lit: how much do you buy the dollar for?

items.en: I'd like to change some euros.
Where is there a cash machine?
items.note: Iranian ATMs only work with Iranian cards.

sections.title: Time and dates
sections.intro: Iran keeps its own solar calendar: the year begins at Nowruz, on the spring equinox around 21 March, and the twelve months have Persian names – Farvardin, Ordibehesht, Khordād and so on. Ask for the milādi (Western) date when you need it. The week starts on Saturday, and Friday is the day off.

items.fa: تا ساعت ده شب باز هستیم.
items.r: tā sā'at-e dah-e shab bāz hastim.
items.en: We're open until ten at night.

items.note: Spelled like ki?, 'who?' – the context tells you which.
zohr is lunchtime; in smaller towns many shops close from zohr until about five.
The week starts on Saturday, and the next days are counted from it: 'one-shanbe', 'two-shanbe'…
Friday (jom'e) is the weekly day off.
Mehr, the seventh month, begins around 23 September.

items.en: What's the date in the Western calendar?
I'll be there in five minutes.

items.fa: هفته‌ی بعد، ماه بعد، سال بعد
items.r: hafte-ye ba'd, māh-e ba'd, sāl-e ba'd
items.en: next week, next month, next year

sections.title: Asking the way
sections.intro: Iranians give directions generously – sometimes even when they are not sure – so it is worth asking twice. Addresses run from big to small: the main street, then the side street (kuche), then the alley, then the number; squares (meydān) and well-known landmarks matter more than house numbers.

items.en: Excuse me, where's the nearest metro station?
How do I get to the bazaar?

items.fa: میدان آزادی از کدام طرف است؟
items.r: meydān-e Āzādi az kodām taraf ast?

items.en: Can you show me on the map?

items.note: Show the address written in Persian – street names in Latin letters mean little to most people.

items.fa: نه، نزدیک است. پنج دقیقه پیاده.
items.r: na, nazdik ast. panj daghighe piyāde.
items.en: No, it's close – five minutes on foot.
How far is it from here?
on the left, on the right

items.fa: همین خیابان را بگیرید و بروید.
items.r: hamin khiyābān rā be-girid o be-ravid.

items.en: After the bridge, the first side street.
At the end of the alley, on the right.

items.note: Public toilets are often the squat kind; carry tissues.

items.en: North or south of the city?
items.note: In Tehran, north also means uphill, towards the mountains.

sections.title: Taxis and the metro
sections.intro: Most people in Tehran get around by ride-hailing app – Snapp or Tapsi – or by metro. Street taxis work in two ways: shared taxis run along fixed routes and pick up passengers on the way, while darbast means you hire the whole car. With a street taxi, agree the fare before you get in.

items.en: Private hire! (I'll take the whole car.)
items.note: Call it to a passing taxi; otherwise the driver may treat you as a shared-taxi passenger.

items.fa: دربست تا میدان ونک چقدر می‌شود؟
items.r: darbast tā meydān-e Vanak cheghadr mi-shavad?
items.en: How much is a private ride to Vanak Square?
items.col: دربست تا میدون ونک چقدر می‌شه؟
items.colR: darbast tā meydun-e Vanak cheghadr mi-she?

items.en: Are you going to Tajrish? (to a shared-taxi driver)

items.note: Snapp and Tapsi are Iran's ride-hailing apps; the name is used like 'an Uber'.

items.en: Excuse me, are you my Snapp?
I'll get out at the corner.
Where do I buy a metro ticket?
I'd like to top up my card.

items.fa: برای رفتن به تجریش کدام خط را سوار شوم؟
items.r: barā-ye raftan be Tajrish kodām khat rā savār shavam?
items.en: Which line do I take for Tajrish?
items.col: برای تجریش کدوم خط رو سوار شم؟
items.colR: barā-ye Tajrish kodum khat ro savār sham?

items.en: Where do I have to change?

items.fa: این قطار به تئاتر شهر می‌رود؟
items.r: in ghatār be Te'ātr-e Shahr mi-ravad?
items.en: Does this train go to Teatr-e Shahr?

items.note: On Tehran metro trains the carriages at each end are reserved for women; women may also ride in the others.

items.fa: اتوبوس فرودگاه از کجا حرکت می‌کند؟
items.r: otobus-e forudgāh az kojā harekat mi-konad?
items.en: Where does the airport bus leave from?
items.col: اتوبوس فرودگاه از کجا حرکت می‌کنه؟
items.colR: otobus-e forudgāh az kojā harekat mi-kone?

sections.title: At the hotel
sections.intro: Hotels ask for your passport at check-in. In the old cities – Yazd, Kashan, Isfahan – look for a traditional-house hotel, a restored courtyard home; on a budget, ask for a mosāferkhāne, a simple guest house.

items.en: Do you have a room free?

items.fa: یک اتاق دو تخته برای سه شب می‌خواهم.
items.r: yek otāgh-e do takhte barā-ye se shab mi-khāham.
items.en: I'd like a room for two for three nights.
items.col: یه اتاق دو تخته برای سه شب می‌خوام.
items.colR: ye otāgh-e do takhte barā-ye se shab mi-khām.
items.note: A single room is yek takhte.

items.en: How much is it per night?
May I have your passport, please?
items.note: lotf mi-konid? – 'will you do the kindness?' – is the polite way to ask for something.

items.en: The air conditioning in my room doesn't work.
Could you bring a clean towel?
Do you have a quieter room?

items.fa: کلید اتاق سیصد و دوازده، لطفاً.
items.r: kelid-e otāgh-e sisad o davāzdah, lotfan.

items.en: Can I leave my suitcase here?
Is there a cheap guest house near here?
